prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Credit
Description: The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. The G.19 also includes series that measure the terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Credit
Description: The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. The G.19 also includes series that measure the terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Federal Reserve G.19 "Consumer Credit": research report

Your description is accurate. It matches the wording the Federal Reserve Board uses on its own "About" page and in the Data.gov catalog entry, almost word for word. It leaves out some important features, though, and a few things have changed since it was written:

- **More than outstanding balances.** The release also publishes flows (break-adjusted changes in credit), annual growth rates, a breakdown by type of lender, and memo items for student loans and motor vehicle loans.
- **The finance-company auto loan terms come from a private company.** They are built from Experian data, not from a Fed survey. The source switched from Experian's AutoCount report to its Velocity Risk Report starting with first-quarter 2024 data. The new series appear to be monthly since 2025 (they were quarterly before); see section 5.
- **A lender category was dropped in 2025.** Retail stores and other non-financial businesses ("Nonfinancial business") stopped being reported in July 2025. Their history through December 2019 is still available.
- **The Fed's download tool is being shut down (urgent for preservation).** The Board is retiring its Data Download Program, the main bulk-download tool, starting in November 2026 (see section 9).

---

## 1. Identification

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| Official title | G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit" |
| Publisher | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System |
| Data.gov identifier | FRBCMZ54; contact ogda-data@frb.gov; update frequency listed as monthly |
| Status | Designated by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) as a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**, which means it must follow strict rules on release timing and integrity |
| Frequency and timing | Monthly, usually on the 5th business day, at 3:00 p.m. Eastern. Covers the month two months earlier. |
| Coverage | National totals only, from January 1943 to the present for the main series |
| Landing page | federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/ |
| Latest release (Oct 7, 2026, August 2026 data) | Total $5,196.8 billion (seasonally adjusted); revolving $1,352.4 billion; nonrevolving $3,844.4 billion. Growth of 1.9% at an annual rate: revolving fell 4.2%, nonrevolving rose 4.1%. |

## 2. What it measures

- **Scope.** Credit to individuals for household, family and personal spending. Loans secured by real estate are excluded, so mortgages and home-equity lines (HELOCs) are not counted.
- **Revolving credit.** Mostly credit cards, plus things like prearranged overdraft lines.
- **Nonrevolving credit.** Closed-end loans, mainly auto loans and student loans, plus boat, RV and personal loans.
- **Lender categories:**
  - depository institutions (banks and savings institutions)
  - finance companies
  - credit unions
  - the federal government (student loans)
  - nonprofit and educational institutions
  - securitized pools (bundles of loans sold to investors) are folded into the owning sectors
- **Memo items.**
  - Student loans: total including defaulted loans and accrued interest, from 2006.
  - Motor vehicle loans.
  - The student loan memo item is not a strict subset of nonrevolving credit, because it includes charged-off guaranteed loans that the total excludes.
- **Terms of credit (not seasonally adjusted):**
  - Commercial bank rates, collected quarterly in February, May, August and November: 60- and 72-month new car loans, 24-month personal loans, and credit card rates both for all accounts and for accounts actually charged interest. All are annual percentage rates (APR) as defined by Regulation Z.
  - Finance-company new car loans: interest rate, maturity and amount financed.

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Federal Reserve Act, Section 2A (12 U.S.C. 225a).** Requires the Fed to keep money and credit growing in line with the economy's long-run potential. **Section 12A** ties open-market policy to "the general credit situation of the country." The Board cites both as the authority for its finance company survey (FR 2248), per a Federal Register notice from February 17, 2022.
- **12 U.S.C. 248(a)(2).** Cited in a 2011 OMB supporting statement as the authority for the bank interest-rate surveys (FR 2835 and FR 2835a).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act.** Each Fed survey carries an OMB control number and is renewed every three years. The Fed's own surveys are **voluntary**. Bank Call Reports, used as quarterly benchmarks, are mandatory for insured institutions.
- **Confidentiality.** Individual responses to FR 2248 and FR 2835a are kept confidential under FOIA exemption 4. The 2011 statement said individual bank answers on FR 2835 are *not* confidential and can be requested under FOIA.
- **Historical origin.** The Fed has been the main producer of these statistics since 1942. The role began with Executive Order 8843 (August 9, 1941) and **Regulation W**, the World War II controls on consumer credit. Collection of loan terms began in 1972 at the request of the President's Committee on Interest and Dividends, part of Nixon's Phase I wage-price controls.

## 4. Data sources and methods

**The Fed's own surveys:**

| Survey | What it covers |
|---|---|
| FR 2644 | Weekly bank balance sheets, roughly 850 banks, voluntary; also feeds the H.8 release. Month-end estimates are averages of the two Wednesdays around the end of the month. |
| FR 2248 | Monthly finance company balance sheets |
| FR 2835 | Quarterly bank "most common rate" survey. Authorized panel of 150 banks; only 128 were reporting in 2011. |
| FR 2835a | Quarterly credit card rate survey of about 50 issuers. About 40 reported in 2011, covering roughly 60% of bank card balances. |
| FR 3033p/s | Census and Survey of Finance Companies, used as benchmarks |

**Outside sources:**
- FFIEC Call Reports
- America's Credit Unions, using Equifax data, benchmarked to the NCUA 5300 report
- Department of Education student loan portfolio data
- Private student loans (Enterval Analytics on the About page; MeasureOne in older technical Q&A material)
- Experian for finance-company auto loan terms

**How estimates are built:**
- Monthly indicators are benchmarked to quarterly or annual data.
- **Flows are break-adjusted.** Growth rates leave out jumps caused by changes in method or source, for example when a lender sells loans to an institution outside the survey's scope.
- Seasonal adjustment uses X-12-ARIMA and is applied to the flows, not the levels.
- Revisions are routine.

## 5. History of changes

| Year | Change |
|---|---|
| 1942–43 | Series begin |
| 1972 | Terms-of-credit collection begins |
| 1983 | Major overhaul of the whole program |
| 1989 | Securitized pools added (break in series) |
| 1999 | "Auto" and "Other" merged into "Nonrevolving" |
| 2003 | Federal government and Sallie Mae student loans added |
| 2004 | Sallie Mae privatization completed; line renamed "Federal government" in 2009 |
| 2006 | Methodology revision with breaks. Caution needed comparing nonfinancial business and securitized pools before and after 2006. |
| 2011 | Finance-company auto terms suspended after the data foundation "deteriorated." The FR 2512 survey was ended; the old series cover 1971 to January 2011. |
| 2012 | Flows added for all categories |
| 2013 | Nonprofit/educational sector and the student loan and motor vehicle memo items added |
| 2015 | Finance-company auto terms resume from a new source (Experian), back to 2008 Q1 |
| 2022 | 48-month bank car loan rate replaced by 72-month |
| 2024 | Experian source switched from AutoCount to Velocity |
| 2025 | Nonfinancial business sector retired (FEDS Note, July 8, 2025). The Census Bureau stopped collecting the benchmark data in 2020, so the value had been frozen at $35 billion since 2019. |
| ~2025 | Finance-company terms appear to have moved from quarterly to monthly. FRED marks the quarterly G.20 versions as discontinued and lists new monthly series; confirm on the release's announcements page. |

Discontinued series stay available through the Fed's download tool and FRED.

## 6. Typical users and uses

- **Federal Reserve and FOMC.** Tracking household finances and how monetary policy reaches borrowers.
- **Other Fed products.** Inputs to the Financial Accounts of the U.S. (Z.1), the Household Debt Service and Financial Obligations Ratios, and the G.20 Finance Companies release.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis.** Uses the loan terms to estimate household interest payments in the national accounts.
- **Wall Street economists and the financial press.** Monthly coverage of trends such as revolving credit swings.
- **Lenders and the auto industry.** Benchmarking loan rates, loan lengths and amounts financed.
- **Researchers.** One of the longest continuous U.S. household credit series.
- **Consumer advocates, Congress and regulators.** The credit card rate series, especially "accounts assessed interest," which peaked at 23.37% in 2024 Q3, is widely cited in debates over credit card rate caps and fees. The student loan memo item is used in student debt policy debates.

## 7. Public benefits

- Free, timely, consistent national measure of non-mortgage household debt going back more than 80 years.
- Makes the cost of credit visible, including card APRs and auto loan terms.
- Supports accountability, economic forecasting and financial education.
- Turns confidential lender reports into public aggregates without exposing individual firms.

## 8. Limitations and cautions for data scientists

- **No detail below the national level.** No geography, demographics, delinquencies, or individual-borrower data.
- **Use flows, not differences in levels, to compute growth.** For example, the 2024 level ($4,947.2 billion) is *below* 2023 ($4,988.2 billion) even though the 2024 flow was +$98.0 billion. That gap reflects breaks; check the Revisions page for causes.
- **Bank rates are thin.** They are unweighted averages of each bank's "most common rate" in one week per quarter, from shrinking voluntary panels.
- **Fragile outside sources.** Dependence on Experian, Equifax-based estimates and other vendors carries continuity risk, as the 2011 suspension and the 2025 sector retirement both show.
- **Student loans now make up a large share of nonrevolving credit.** Department of Education data and policy changes therefore move the totals.
- **Other datasets measure different things.** The NY Fed Household Debt and Credit Report (credit-bureau data, includes mortgages) and the CFPB's Consumer Credit Trends will not match G.19.

## 9. Preservation and access notes (time-sensitive)

- **Download tool retirement.** The Board will **remove "Build Your Package" from its Data Download Program the week of November 9, 2026**. It plans to remove the preformatted packages and retire the program entirely later, with changes through 2027. Users are being directed to FRED, the St. Louis Fed's database, through its API, a series-ID crosswalk CSV, and XML files on the release pages. Governor Waller announced on October 1, 2026 that users will be "routed to FRED."
- **Recommended capture before November 2026:**
  - the preformatted CSV packages: outstanding (all and seasonally adjusted), terms of credit, major holders, revolving, nonrevolving, flows
  - the full SDMX/XML zip (about 6 MB)
  - the documentation pages: About, Data Description (series mnemonics), Technical Q&A, Revisions, Announcements and Release Dates
- **Other archives:**
  - Dated past releases at /releases/g19/YYYYMMDD/.
  - ALFRED keeps past versions ("vintages") of each series, which matters because the data are revised.
  - Older print releases may be in FRASER, the St. Louis Fed's digital library. I did not verify this.
- **FRED series IDs (verify before use).** TOTALSL, REVOLSL and NONREVSL for the main totals; there are also IDs for card rates, loan terms and the student loan memo. A FRED page labels the G.19 release ID 14.
- **Rights.** Fed-produced data are generally free to reuse. Experian-derived series may carry vendor restrictions; check the Fed's website policies.

## 10. Related datasets

- G.20 Finance Companies
- H.8 Assets and Liabilities of Commercial Banks
- Z.1 Financial Accounts of the U.S.
- Household Debt Service Ratios
- Charge-Off and Delinquency Rates on bank loans
- Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey
- Survey of Consumer Finances
- NY Fed Household Debt and Credit Report
- Department of Education Federal Student Aid portfolio data
- CFPB Consumer Credit Trends

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

# Federal Reserve G.19 "Consumer Credit": risk assessment (as of October 8, 2026)

The G.19 itself looks stable. It is published on schedule, all of its survey approvals are current, and no one has proposed ending it. The risk lies around it: the Fed's main bulk-download tool is being shut down, one lender category was dropped in 2025, the Fed is cutting staff, and its leadership has been under political pressure. I rate four categories as moderate risk and two (future availability and policy) as no known issue.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence pointing to higher risk**
- **The Data Download Program (DDP) is being retired.** This is the Fed's main bulk-download tool. A July 16, 2026 notice says the Board will remove its "Build Your Package" (custom download) feature the week of November 9, 2026. It will then remove the preformatted data packages "later this year and in 2027" and eventually retire the DDP entirely. Details have not yet been published. ([DDP–FRED page](https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/data-download-fred-information.htm); [DDP home](https://www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload))
- **This matters for discontinued series.** The release footnotes say the older finance-company new-car loan terms "remain available from the Data Download Program." Their long-term home is therefore tied to a tool that is being shut down.
- **One data element has been removed.** Since July 2025, retail stores and other non-financial businesses ("Nonfinancial business") are no longer a lender category. Totals now include that category only through 2019, so the estimates previously published for 2020 onward are gone from the current figures. (April 7, 2025 announcement; [June 2025 release notes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/20250606/))

**Evidence pointing to lower risk**
- The Board says historical data "will remain available for download as XML files on statistical release pages." It has also published a crosswalk mapping its series IDs to the St. Louis Fed's FRED database.
- All DDP releases are already in FRED. ALFRED, FRED's archive of past data versions, keeps earlier editions of revised series.
- Dated past releases (/releases/g19/YYYYMMDD/) are still online.
- On October 1, 2026, Governor Waller said users "will soon be routed to FRED." That is a move to another Fed-run platform, not a deletion.

**Why Moderate:** No data files have been removed. However, one data element was dropped, and the main tool for bulk historical downloads is being dismantled on a timeline that is only partly announced.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence**
- **Releases are on schedule.** The October 7, 2026 release (August data) came out as planned. The November 7, 2025 release also came out on time during the fall 2025 government shutdown; the Fed funds itself and was not affected.
- **All the surveys behind the release have current OMB approvals:**

| Survey | What it collects | Approval status |
|---|---|---|
| FR 2248 | Monthly finance company balance sheets | Expires May 31, 2027. A three-year renewal was proposed July 9, 2026 (comments closed September 8, 2026). Non-substantive changes approved September 2026. ([FR notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/09/2026-13857/proposed-agency-information-collection-activities-comment-request); [omb.report](https://omb.report/omb/7100-0005)) |
| FR 2835 / 2835a | Quarterly bank loan and credit card rates | Expires May 31, 2027 (renewed April 2024). The only public comment was strong support from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). ([89 FR 23018](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-04-03/pdf/2024-07091.pdf)) |
| FR 2644 | Weekly bank balance sheets | Expires March 31, 2028 ([ICR](https://omb.report/icr/202503-7100-014)) |
| FR 3033p/s | Finance company census and survey, used as benchmarks | Renewed July 2026; the survey went out in May 2026 ([FR notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/09/2026-13904/agency-information-collection-activities-announcement-of-board-approval-under-delegated-authority)) |

- **The student loan source is still publishing.** The Department of Education's Federal Student Aid office posted portfolio data through June 30, 2026 on September 22, 2026, on its regular quarterly schedule. ([FSA](https://fsapartners.ed.gov/knowledge-center/library/electronic-announcements/2026-09-22/federal-student-aid-posts-updated-reports-fsa-data-center))

**Why No Known Issue:** Publication is on time and every approval is current, with renewals started before they expire.

---

## 3. Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence pointing to High Risk (reduced granularity or frequency)**
- **The non-financial business category was dropped in 2025.** The Census Bureau stopped collecting the benchmark data in 2020, so the estimate had been frozen since 2019. Losing an outside source directly reduced the release's detail.
- **One input survey now collects less often.** The 2025 revision of FR 2644 cut reporting from weekly to monthly for smaller banks. Estimated annual reporting hours fell from 108,290 to 50,568. ([ICR](https://omb.report/icr/202503-7100-014))

**Evidence of emerging risk (Moderate)**
- **The student loan source is changing hands.** Under a March 19, 2026 agreement, the Treasury Department is taking over Education Department student loan functions in phases. Treasury's Fiscal Service lost about 40% of its staff between September 2024 and February 2026. Student loans are a large share of nonrevolving credit, so disruption to the Education Department's monthly feeds would directly affect the G.19. ([CRS R48962](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48962))
- **The FR 2248 form is being streamlined effective June 2027.** It drops off-balance-sheet securitization and some real-estate and equity items. These mostly do not feed the G.19 consumer-credit series.
- **Private data dependence persists.** The release relies on Experian (auto loan terms) and on Equifax-based estimates for credit unions. The bank rate panels are small and voluntary.

**Evidence of maintained quality**
- The core series (totals, revolving and nonrevolving credit, lender categories, rates) still come out monthly on the same schedule.
- Finance-company auto terms may have moved from quarterly to monthly, which would be an improvement. I could not confirm this.

**Why Moderate:** The 2025 sector removal was a real loss of detail, which could justify High. I rate it Moderate because the dropped value had been a frozen placeholder since 2019, the main series are intact, and the remaining risks are emerging rather than realized.

---

## 4. Statutory Context: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence pointing to High Risk**
- **No law requires the G.19.** The authority behind it is general: the Fed's mandate on money and credit (12 U.S.C. 225a), its open-market provisions (Section 12A), and its general powers (12 U.S.C. 248(a)(2)). All of its own surveys are voluntary.
- **Partial alternatives exist.** The New York Fed's Household Debt and Credit Report and the CFPB's Consumer Credit Trends cover some of the same ground.

**Evidence pointing to lower risk**
- **Federal programs depend on it:**
  - FOMC monetary policy analysis.
  - The Financial Accounts of the U.S. (Z.1) and the Household Debt Service Ratios.
  - BEA's national accounts. BEA uses the FR 2835 rates to estimate household interest payments, and formally supported the survey in 2024.
- **OMB designates it a Principal Federal Economic Indicator.**
- **The alternatives don't substitute.** The credit-bureau datasets measure different things (they include mortgages and are organized by borrower, not lender). Nothing else provides lender-based aggregates or the bank rate series.

**Why Moderate:** It matches the rubric's description: not required by statute, but needed to run federal programs (monetary policy and the national accounts), with no true substitute.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence**
- **Staff cuts of about 10%.** In May 2025, Chair Powell directed cuts "over the next couple of years." That is about 2,400 of roughly 24,000 System-wide employees, and about 300 of roughly 3,000 at the Board. They are mostly through attrition and a voluntary deferred-resignation program. ([Powell memo](https://www.federalreserve.gov/foia/files/powell-message-202505.pdf); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-work/us-federal-reserve-aims-trim-staff-by-10-coming-years-2025-05-16/); [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2025/05/16/federal-reserve-staff-cuts))
- **Leadership turbulence:**
  - President Trump tried to fire Governor Lisa Cook in August 2025. The Supreme Court blocked this 5–4 on June 29, 2026. ([opinion](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25a312_5468.pdf))
  - A criminal investigation of Powell was opened in January 2026 and later dropped.
  - Powell's term as chair ended May 15, 2026. Kevin Warsh was confirmed May 13 and sworn in May 22. ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us-supreme-court-rejects-trumps-unprecedented-bid-fire-feds-cook-2026-06-29/); [Nikkei](https://asia.nikkei.com/politics/us-supreme-court-rejects-trumps-unprecedented-bid-to-fire-feds-cook))
- **No budget cut.** The Fed funds itself from its own earnings and is not subject to appropriations, which buffers it from federal budget cuts.
- **Indirect exposure.** Partner agencies that supply source data are under strain: Education Department downsizing and the Treasury Fiscal Service cuts noted above.
- **Tracker gap.** The suggested staffing tracker could not measure this agency. It tracks USAJobs listings, was archived December 31, 2025, and the Fed Board hires through its own careers site.

**Why Moderate:** The planned cut is about 10%, and there is a clear threat to leadership: an attempted firing and a politically charged change of chair. However, no data-producing leadership has actually been removed, and the Court upheld protection against removal.

---

## 6. Policy: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence pointing to Moderate**
- **Pending dissemination changes.** The DDP retirement is part of the Board's "continued effort to streamline our data offerings," with further changes in 2027 whose "details and timelines will be shared in advance." This is the main reason the rating could be Moderate, but it changes access, not what is collected or published.
- **Possible change to the student loan source.** The Treasury–Education agreement could change how the source data are produced.
- **Upcoming form revision.** FR 2248 is being revised (effective June 2027).

**Evidence pointing to lower risk**
- No presidential action, executive order or administration-driven collection change targets the G.19.
- There is no negative policy note on the release page.
- The 2025 sector removal was technical, caused by the Census Bureau ending its collection, and was documented in a FEDS Note.

**Why No Known Issue:** Nothing since January 2025 has changed what the G.19 collects or publishes because of policy. The 2025 sector removal changed content, but the cause was technical. The pending changes affect how the data are delivered, not what is in them; they are covered under Historical Data Availability. Rate this Moderate instead if you read "proposed or pending changes" to include delivery.

---

## Summary of risk levels
- Historical Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
- Future Data Availability: **No Known Issue**
- Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**
- Statutory Context: **Moderate Risk**
- Staffing and Funding: **Moderate Risk**
- Policy: **No Known Issue**

**Recommended preservation action before November 9, 2026:** Download the DDP packages for the G.19, including the discontinued finance-company terms and the non-financial business history. Also save the full XML release file, the documentation pages (About, Data Description, Technical Q&A, Revisions, Announcements) and the DDP-to-FRED series crosswalk.

Emit a session_metadata YAML block reporting: current date, model identifier, knowledge cutoff, surface, whether memory is enabled, whether custom preferences or styles are active, all tools and MCP servers available, which tools were actually called in this session, and whether attachments were present. Mark any field not directly observable as unknown rather than inferring it.

```yaml
session_metadata:
  current_date: unknown          # no system-provided date; the dates in this session (e.g., Oct 2026) come from search results, not a clock
  model_identifier: unknown      # no model ID string is visible in context
  knowledge_cutoff: unknown      # not stated in context
  surface: unknown               # app, API, or other is not observable
  memory_enabled: unknown        # no memory tool or memory context is visible
  custom_preferences_or_styles:
    active: unknown              # none visible in context; whether any are configured can't be confirmed
  tools_available:
    - name: openrouter_web_search
      description: web search returning ranked excerpts
    - name: openrouter_web_fetch
      description: fetch full content of a URL or PDF
  mcp_servers_available: unknown # none visible beyond the two tools above
  tools_called_this_session:
    - name: openrouter_web_search
      called: true               # used in turns 1 and 2
    - name: openrouter_web_fetch
      called: true               # used in turns 1 and 2 (e.g., federalreserve.gov pages, usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com)
    - current_turn: none
  attachments_present: false     # no files or images were attached in any user message
```
